title: Surface preparation and washing
audience: Painters and painting workers who prepare surfaces for painting
learningOutcomes: Wash and clean a surface so that paint can key and adhere.
Choose a washing method suited to the surface and the contamination.
Dry and check the surface before the first coat, and stop where damp is present.

instruction.heading: Why the surface comes first
instruction.body: Paint bonds to the layer beneath it. If that layer is dirty, greasy, chalky, mouldy, wet or already flaking, the bond is weak, and the paint will lift, blister or peel, often within months. Preparation is therefore part of the paint system, not an optional extra. Most early paint failures trace back to the surface rather than to the paint itself. Before any cleaner goes on, you need to know what the surface is made of, what has been on it, and whether it is sound enough to take a new coat. A clean, dry and sound surface gives the next coat something to grip, and the time spent preparing it is what makes the finish last.

instruction.heading: Inspect and record the contamination
instruction.body: Inspect the surface in good daylight or with a torch held low across it, because flat light hides dull films and fine marks. Look for grease, especially on kitchen and bathroom walls, near cooking areas and around switches. Rub a dry finger across the surface: a fine powder on the finger suggests chalking, which is breakdown of the paint film and needs removing before painting. Look for efflorescence, the white crystalline deposit that can appear on masonry and render, which is usually salt brought to the surface by moisture. Look for mould, which may appear as dark spots, fuzz or a musty patch, and for dust, loose paint and old wax or silicone residue. Tap or lightly scrape the paint to find areas that are loose or flaking. Check for damp by eye and with a moisture meter where the site provides one, and note any stain that suggests water is coming from behind the surface. Record each finding with its location, because each one changes the method.

instruction.heading: Choosing a washing method
instruction.body: Match the method to the contamination. Water and a neutral detergent, applied with a sponge or cloth and rinsed with clean water, suits dust and light soiling on most interior and exterior surfaces. A stronger alkaline cleaner, used only as the product data sheet directs, is used for greasy walls and for removing residue that water does not lift. Chalking and loose powder are usually brushed or wiped off before washing, so that the powder does not smear. Efflorescence is brushed dry first, and then washed, because wetting it first can draw the salt back into the surface. Loose or flaking paint is removed mechanically with scraping or sanding, and this brings in a dust control problem and, on older surfaces, a lead or asbestos question. Where a surface may be old enough to contain lead or asbestos, stop and refer it before any mechanical removal, using “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)”. Do not mix cleaning products. Check each product's safety data sheet and label before use, and keep to the dilution the product states.

instruction.heading: Pressure, water and what it can damage
instruction.body: Water is the main washing tool, and it can also be the main cause of damage. High-pressure washing can strip sound paint, roughen old timber, damage render and mortar, loosen fixings, and drive water behind cladding, flashings and window frames. Once water is behind a surface, it can show up later as a stain, a blister or rot, and the cause is then hard to trace back to the wash. Use the lowest pressure that does the job, keep the nozzle moving, and keep a sensible distance from the surface. Do not aim the water into vents, gaps, under sills, at switchboards, power outlets or light fittings, or at gaps around window frames. Keep water away from electrical fittings at all times. Any pressure figure used on a job is a site setting checked against the product and surface, and no figure is given in this lesson. Where the pressure needed to remove a contaminant would damage the surface, stop and choose a gentler method, or refer.

instruction.heading: Mould and damp: stop and refer
instruction.body: Mould is not a surface finish problem to paint over. Where mould or damp is found, stop painting that area and record it. Mould can show the presence of water, condensation or a building fault, and painting over it hides the evidence and tends to fail. Cleaning mould is a separate task with its own controls, and it is covered by the mould guidance in “Moisture ingress and mould warning signs”. Do not paint until the moisture source is known and dealt with, or until the client has agreed in writing to a stated scope. Check the surface for damp after it has been washed and dried, because a surface that looks dry at the surface may still be wet behind.

instruction.heading: Drying, checking and protecting the job
instruction.body: Rinse the surface with clean water to remove detergent, because any residue left on the surface can stop paint from bonding. Allow the surface to dry fully before the next step. The drying time depends on the surface, the temperature, the humidity and the wind, and the product data sheet for the first coat states the conditions it needs. A surface that feels dry may still hold moisture in its core, so check with a moisture meter where the site provides one, or by a method the product data sheet accepts. Before washing, protect the floor, fittings and adjacent surfaces with drop sheets and masking. Cover power outlets and switches where water could reach them, and keep the wash water away from open windows and doors. Wash runoff can carry detergent into stormwater or gardens.

instruction.heading: The limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant a painting licence, a plastering licence, a lead or asbestos removal licence or any authority to undertake regulated work. Licence positions depend on the state, the value of the work and the scope, and they are set out in the safety and regulatory section below and in “Paint systems, primers and coverage” and “Painting quotes, variations and colour approval”.

procedure: Inspect the surface in good light and record grease, chalking, efflorescence, mould, dust, loose paint and any sign of damp, with the location of each finding.
Stop and refer, without disturbing the surface, if the surface may be an older painted surface, if mould is present, or if the contamination is unknown.
Choose the washing method for the surface and the contamination, and check the product's data sheet and dilution.
Protect the floor, fittings, openings and electrical outlets, and keep water away from them.
Brush off chalk and efflorescence first, then wash from the bottom of the surface upwards, using the lowest effective water pressure.
Rinse with clean water until no detergent residue remains, and let the surface dry fully.
Check the surface for damp by eye and with a moisture meter where provided, and record the result before any paint is opened.
Record the washing method, the product, the rinse and the drying check on the surface preparation record.

workedExamples.situation: A greasy kitchen wall is to be painted, and the client asks you to skip washing to save time.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the wall be painted without washing?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Grease stops paint from bonding, so the new coat will lift early even if it looks fine on the day. Explain to the client that the washing is part of the paint job and is what makes the finish last. Wash the wall with a suitable cleaner, rinse it with clean water, and let it dry fully. Check it for any remaining film by wiping a dry cloth across it. Record the washing method and the drying check on the preparation record before opening the paint.

workedExamples.situation: An exterior rendered wall has white crystalline deposits in patches, and a dark fuzzy growth in the shaded corner. The owner asks for a high-pressure wash and a quick coat of paint.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct sequence, and what do you refuse?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the high-pressure wash and the quick coat. The deposits look like efflorescence, which should be brushed off dry before any wetting, and the growth looks like mould, which is a stop-and-refer condition. Record both findings with their locations, check the wall for damp, and refer the mould before any painting. Do not paint until the source of the moisture is known and the client has agreed in writing to a stated scope, with the mould and any efflorescence treatment noted as excluded where they are not part of the quote.

workedExamples.situation: A timber window frame in a house shows bare patches and loose paint at the joints. The owner says the paint is only a few years old, but the house is a much older building.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you sand the loose paint off the frame now?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not until the older paint question is answered. Mechanical removal, such as sanding or scraping, can release dust, and on older buildings the paint may contain lead. The owner's word about when the paint was applied is not an assessment. Stop, keep dust contained, and refer the frame to the assessment route in “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)” before any removal. Record the findings, the owner's statement, and the referral.

equipmentAndPpe: Buckets, sponges, soft brushes and cleaning cloths
Scraper and brush for removing chalk, efflorescence and loose material, used only on surfaces that are assessed as suitable
Cleaner suitable for the surface, with its safety data sheet and dilution available
Clean rinse water and a low-pressure applicator, with the pressure setting noted
Moisture meter, where the site provides one
Torch for low-angle light across the surface
Drop sheets, masking tape and protective covers for fittings and openings
Gloves and eye protection suitable for the cleaner, as the data sheet specifies
Respiratory protection for dust, used only where the site's dust assessment requires it, with a fit check

commonErrors.error: Skipping washing on greasy or dirty surfaces to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Wash, rinse and dry the surface before painting. Record the step.

commonErrors.error: Using high-pressure water on old paint, render, timber or near fittings.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the lowest effective method, keep the nozzle moving, and keep water away from openings and electrical fittings.

commonErrors.error: Painting over damp, mould or unknown contamination.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the finding, and refer before any paint is applied.

commonErrors.error: Leaving detergent residue on the surface after washing.
commonErrors.prevention: Rinse with clean water until the residue is gone, and check the surface before painting.

commonErrors.error: Wetting efflorescence before brushing it off.
commonErrors.prevention: Brush the deposit off dry first, and then wash.
Use one product at a time, as its data sheet directs, and rinse between products where the data sheet calls for it.

commonErrors.error: Sanding older paint to see whether it is lead.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not disturb an older surface before it has been assessed. Refer it under “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)”.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Painting licence positions by state (owner answer 2026-11-04; checked 2026-11-06): New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork have not needed one since 2015 unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source.

Older surfaces may contain lead, and disturbing them needs assessment before any sanding, scraping, heat stripping or blasting. See “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)”. Asbestos may be present in some older materials, and the asbestos limits are set out in “Lead paint and older-surface awareness (refer)”.

Mould removal and damp investigation are outside this lesson. Refer to the mould guidance in “Moisture ingress and mould warning signs” and to the property owner's responsibility for the building fault.
Check the local rule before washing outdoors.
Completing this lesson does not give a painting, plastering or asbestos licence, certificate or authority.

qualityStandard: The surface is clean, dry and sound before the first coat, and the check is recorded.
The washing method is recorded, suited to the surface and the contamination, and matches the product's data sheet.
No paint is applied over damp, mould, efflorescence not removed, or unknown contamination.
documentationEvidence: Surface preparation record with the inspection findings, their locations, the washing method, the product name, the rinse and the drying check.
Record of any damp, mould, older-surface or contamination finding, with the referral and the owner's written decision.
Photographs of the surface before and after preparation, taken with the owner's permission.
summary: Clean and dry the surface before painting, because paint fails on greasy, chalky, mouldy or wet surfaces.
Choose the washing method for the surface, and keep high pressure away from old, fragile and electrical areas.
Stop and refer damp, mould, older painted surfaces and unknown contamination, and record each finding.

knowledgeChecks.question: A greasy wall is to be painted without washing to save time. What is correct?
options: Wash, rinse and dry the wall before painting
Paint it without washing the wall first
Use more coats to cover the grease well
Use a cheaper paint to save the cost here

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is high-pressure water a risk on old paint and render?
options: It makes the paint look shiny and very glossy
It can damage the surface and drive water behind it
It removes the need for primer on the wall surface
It is always safe for every surface type on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: A fine powder comes off on a finger when a wall is rubbed. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Chalking of the surface, which should be removed before painting
A fresh coat of paint that is ready to use on the wall
That the wall is ready to paint as it is right now and needs no prep

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be checked after washing and before the first coat is applied?
options: That the colour is on sale this week
That the ladders are in the van today
That the surface is dry and free of damp
